sections.title: Causes: viral, tuberculous, uraemic and the rest

blocks.text: **Acute pericarditis** is inflammation of the pericardial sac and it can coexist with myocarditis. It accounts for roughly **5% of emergency chest-pain attendances**, is commoner in men (especially young adults), and in most patients **no cause is ever found**. Around 90% of cases are labelled idiopathic, and most of these are assumed to be undiagnosed viral infections. Any form of pericarditis can produce an effusion, which may be fibrinous, serous, haemorrhagic or purulent depending on the cause.

blocks.title: Causes of acute pericarditis and effusion
rows: Coxsackie, echovirus, adenovirus, mumps, EBV, influenza, HIV, SARS-CoV-2
Commonest in young adults, especially men; most "idiopathic" cases are presumed viral
Under 5% in developed countries, but over 50% in developing countries and over 90% in HIV-positive patients; insidious, with constitutional symptoms
Severe pre-terminal uraemia or under-dialysis; "dialysis pericarditis" with intercurrent illness or surgery
Haemorrhagic effusion and atrial arrhythmias; risk of tamponade
Early post-infarct pericarditis; **Dressler syndrome** (autoimmune, weeks to months later)
Bronchial and breast carcinoma, lymphoma (especially Hodgkin), leukaemia, melanoma
Large, often **haemorrhagic** effusion from blocked cardiac lymphatic drainage
Rare: complicates sepsis, spreads from intrathoracic infection, or follows penetrating injury

blocks.title: Other causes to list
items: **Autoimmune / connective tissue:** rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, rheumatic fever, scleroderma, vasculitis
**Drug-induced:** procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ciclosporin
**Physical:** trauma, mediastinal radiation (over 40 Gy), post-pericardiotomy (after cardiac surgery)
**Miscellaneous:** myxoedema, chylopericardium, aortic dissection
**Effusion without inflammation (transudate):** heart failure (especially right-sided), cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism, amyloidosis

blocks.title: Tuberculous pericarditis: why it is emphasised
items: It can complicate known pulmonary TB **or be the first sign** of the infection
Globally, TB is the **commonest cause of pericardial effusion in HIV**; in Africa a tuberculous effusion is a common feature of AIDS
In TB-endemic countries **more than 60% of pericardial effusions** are tuberculous
The effusion often organises and the pericardium thickens, so **constriction is a frequent late outcome**

blocks.title: Uraemic pericarditis
items: Seen with **severe, pre-terminal uraemia** or **inadequate dialysis**; dialysis pericarditis can also arise in a patient on apparently adequate dialysis during an intercurrent illness or after surgery
Pocket Medicine puts its frequency at about **5–13%** of patients before haemodialysis starts and **~20%** of those on chronic haemodialysis
Effusions are often **haemorrhagic** and **atrial arrhythmias** are common; there is a real risk of **tamponade**
Chest pain may be **absent**
Uraemic pericarditis is a recognised **indication for dialysis (RRT)** in both AKI and CKD; with uraemic encephalopathy it is a strong indication in AKI

blocks.text: **Timing after MI:** Davidson places early post-infarct pericarditis **particularly on days 2–3**; Step-Up describes it within the first 24 hours. Follow Davidson. Do not confuse either with **Dressler syndrome**, which appears **weeks to months** after the infarct with fever and pleurisy.

sections.title: Acute pericarditis: symptoms, signs and investigations

blocks.title: Symptoms
items: Sharp **retrosternal pain** radiating to the neck, shoulders and trapezius ridge
Pleuritic and **positional**: worse on deep inspiration, lying flat, coughing, swallowing and movement; **eased by sitting up and leaning forward**
Low-grade fever is common; there may be a preceding viral illness
Pain can be **absent** in TB, malignant, radiation-induced, uraemic and rheumatoid pericarditis

blocks.text: The **pericardial friction rub** is a high-pitched, superficial scratching or crunching noise that is **diagnostic** when heard. It can have up to **three components** (atrial systole, ventricular systole, which is the loudest and most often heard, and early diastole), giving a "to-and-fro" quality. It is best heard at the **lower left sternal border** with the diaphragm, with the patient **sitting up, in expiration**. It is **transient** and varies over hours, so listen repeatedly.
**Two of four** makes the clinical diagnosis: (1) typical pleuritic, positional chest pain; (2) friction rub; (3) typical ECG changes; (4) new or worsening pericardial effusion.

blocks.title: ECG: pericarditis vs STEMI
rows: **Widespread**, anterior and inferior leads together; fits no single coronary territory
Confined to the leads facing the infarct
Reciprocal ST depression in opposite leads
**PR depression** (PR elevation in aVR); a very specific sign
Invert only **after** the ST segments return to baseline
Can invert while ST is still raised

blocks.title: ECG evolution (four stages)
items: **Stage I:** diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
**Stage II:** ST and PR segments normalise (typically around 1 week)
**Stage III:** diffuse T-wave inversion (not in every patient; more likely with some myocarditis)
**Stage IV:** T waves return to normal

blocks.title: Other investigations
items: **CRP, ESR and white cell count** are raised (inflammatory markers up in ~80%) and fall as it settles; a high CRP predicts recurrence
**Troponin / CK** rise in about 30%, signalling **myopericarditis**
**Echocardiography** in every patient to look for an effusion (it may be normal)
**CXR** is usually normal; the silhouette enlarges only with a large effusion (over ~250 mL)
Look for a cause where indicated: urea and creatinine, autoantibodies, HIV test, malignancy screen

blocks.note: Look at: concave ST elevation in both anterior and inferior leads (I, II, aVL, V1–V6), a spread that no single coronary artery explains.
Look at: diffuse concave ST elevation across most leads in acute pericarditis.

blocks.text: **Uraemic pericarditis** is mainly fibrin deposition without epicardial inflammation, so the classic diffuse ST elevation and PR depression are often **absent**. A bland ECG does not exclude it in a patient on dialysis with a rub.

The normal sac holds about **50 mL** of lubricating fluid. **Cardiac tamponade** is acute heart failure caused by compression of the heart by pericardial fluid. **The speed of accumulation matters more than the volume**: around 200 mL of blood collecting quickly after trauma can cause tamponade, while 2 L of malignant fluid may gather slowly because the pericardium has time to stretch.

blocks.title: Causes of tamponade
items: Any pericarditis with a progressive effusion, especially **malignant, tuberculous/infective and uraemic**
**Haemopericardium**: penetrating chest trauma; iatrogenic (central lines, pacing, cardiac procedures)
**Free-wall rupture** after MI
**Aortic dissection** into the pericardium

blocks.title: Effusion vs tamponade at the bedside
rows: Soft, distant heart sounds; apex beat obscured
Rub may fade as fluid separates the layers (not always abolished)
**Grossly raised JVP** with a sharp x descent and blunted or absent y descent
**Ewart sign**: dullness, bronchial breathing and egophony below the left scapular angle (compressed left lung base)
**Pulsus paradoxus**: inspiratory systolic fall of ≥10 mmHg; the pulse may vanish in inspiration
**Clear lung fields** despite shock; narrow pulse pressure

blocks.text: **Beck triad** (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised JVP) is the classic description, but it is **often incomplete**: in one series distant sounds were present in 28%, raised JVP in 76% and hypotension in 26%. Pulsus paradoxus has a sensitivity of about 82%. Shock with a raised JVP and **clear lungs** should make you think of tamponade.

**Why pulsus paradoxus happens:** the fluid fixes the total volume available to both ventricles. In inspiration more blood enters the right ventricle, the septum bulges into the LV, LV filling and stroke volume fall, and systolic pressure drops more than the normal (<10 mmHg).

blocks.title: Investigating effusion and tamponade
rows: Echo-free space (detects as little as ~20 mL). Tamponade: **late diastolic RA collapse, early diastolic RV collapse**, inspiratory septal shift into the LV, dilated IVC collapsing <50% on inspiration, expiratory hepatic-vein flow reversal
Sinus tachycardia, **low-voltage QRS** (<0.5 mV in limb leads), **electrical alternans** (heart swinging in fluid)
Normal until over ~250 mL; then a large **globular / "water-bottle"** heart with sharp borders and **no pulmonary venous congestion**
Loculated effusions (for example after cardiac surgery)
Raised and **equalised diastolic pressures** in all chambers; blunted y descent

blocks.title: Diagnostic pericardiocentesis and biopsy
items: Echo-guided, aseptic aspiration is indicated when a **tuberculous, malignant or purulent** effusion is suspected (also large or recurrent effusions)
Send fluid for cell count, protein, LDH, glucose, Gram stain and culture, **AFB smear and culture, ADA, TB PCR** and **cytology**
TB is confirmed by finding or culturing tubercle bacilli in the fluid
**Pericardial biopsy** if TB or malignancy is suspected and the aspirate is non-diagnostic; take one at every surgical drainage

blocks.title: Managing tamponade
items: A **medical emergency**: echo-guided **percutaneous pericardiocentesis** as soon as possible, usually with dramatic improvement; a drain may be left in
Needle route: **below the xiphoid aiming towards the left shoulder**, or medial to the apex
While preparing: cautious IV fluid; **avoid** beta-blockers, vasoconstrictors and positive-pressure ventilation, which worsen filling
**Surgical drainage** for viscous, loculated, haemorrhagic or rapidly re-accumulating effusions
Recurrent (in the UK most often malignant) effusions: **pericardial fenestration** (a window draining into surrounding tissue), done percutaneously or surgically
Stable, non-haemorrhagic tamponade in known renal failure: **dialysis** helps more than aspiration

blocks.title: Effusion without tamponade
items: No routine tap unless a diagnosis is needed; most effusions resolve
Small, insignificant effusions: **repeat echo in 1–2 weeks**
Idiopathic effusions persisting **over 3 months** carry a high risk of tamponade, so consider drainage

blocks.text: If tamponade is due to **aortic dissection or myocardial rupture** (or trauma with continuing bleeding), needle aspiration can provoke **fatal further bleeding**: **emergency surgery** is the treatment of choice. Pericardiocentesis risks also include arrhythmia, coronary artery injury and RV puncture.

blocks.note: Look at: a large circumferential echo-free space surrounding the left ventricle.
Look at: globular cardiac silhouette on CXR; CT confirms circumferential fluid and no pericardial calcification.
Look at: QRS amplitude alternating from beat to beat (electrical alternans) with a large effusion.

blocks.text: In **constrictive pericarditis** the pericardium becomes thickened, fibrosed and often calcified, so the heart sits in a rigid shell and **cannot fill in diastole**. Calcification may extend into the myocardium. It classically **follows TB pericarditis**, but also haemopericardium, viral, rheumatoid, purulent/bacterial and radiation pericarditis, open-heart surgery and dopamine agonists (cabergoline, pergolide). About 1–2% of acute pericarditis progresses to constriction; often the original insult is never identified. Because it develops slowly and is compensated, it is **less immediately dangerous than tamponade**.

**Physiology:** early diastolic filling is rapid and then stops abruptly when the stiff pericardium is reached. That sudden halt produces the **pericardial knock**, the **rapid y descent** and the "dip-and-plateau" ventricular pressure trace. In tamponade, by contrast, filling is impaired **throughout** diastole.

blocks.title: Clinical features (a right-heart-failure picture)
items: Fatigue; rapid, low-volume pulse
**Raised JVP with a rapid, prominent y descent**; **Kussmaul sign** (JVP rises in inspiration)
**Pericardial knock**: loud early diastolic sound
**Marked ascites and hepatomegaly**, peripheral oedema
**AF is common** (up to a third in advanced cases)
Breathlessness is **not prominent** because the lungs are seldom congested

blocks.text: Suspect constriction in **unexplained right heart failure with a small heart**, and in an apparently "cirrhotic" patient with ascites and hepatomegaly who also has **distended neck veins**. It causes post-hepatic portal hypertension and **high-SAAG ascites**.

blocks.title: Investigations
rows: Relatively **small heart**; **pericardial calcification** in up to 50% (a lateral film helps); TB is the commonest cause of calcification
Low-voltage QRS, generalised T flattening or inversion; AF
Thick or calcified pericardium, small ventricles, **septal bounce**, exaggerated respiratory variation in inflow
**Equal LV and RV end-diastolic pressures**, dip-and-plateau (square-root) sign, LV/RV pressure discordance with respiration

blocks.title: Management
items: Treat the diastolic heart failure with **loop diuretics** and **aldosterone antagonists** (spironolactone)
Definitive treatment is **surgical pericardiectomy** (complete resection). Davidson stresses its **high morbidity**, with disappointing results in up to 50%
Kumar advises **early** pericardiectomy in non-tuberculous cases, before severe constriction and myocardial atrophy
**Tuberculous constriction:** if calcified, early pericardiectomy under anti-TB drug cover; if not calcified, anti-TB therapy first and surgery if no improvement after 4–6 weeks

blocks.text: **Kussmaul sign and pulsus paradoxus are not clean discriminators.** Davidson lists **both** signs under tamponade **and** under constriction. Kumar says pulsus occurs in constriction but less often, and Pocket Medicine says it is usually absent there, linking Kussmaul mainly to constriction. Follow Davidson, and discriminate by tempo, the y descent (rapid in constriction, absent in tamponade), heart size and imaging.
A **calcified pericardium is not necessarily constricting**, and **restrictive cardiomyopathy** mimics constriction closely. Telling them apart matters because constriction is surgically curable.

blocks.note: Look at: a heavy shell of pericardial calcification on the lateral chest film in chronic constriction.
Look at: thickened pericardium on short-axis cardiac MRI.
Look at: tuberculous effusion with fibrous strands, a sign that it is organising towards constriction.

sections.title: Managing acute, recurrent and cause-specific pericarditis

blocks.title: Treatment by cause
rows: Davidson: **aspirin 600 mg 6 times daily**, or indometacin 50 mg three times daily if a stronger drug is needed. Kumar: aspirin 750–1000 mg or ibuprofen 600–800 mg three times daily for 1–2 weeks **plus colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily for 3 months**
70–90% self-limiting; recovery over days to weeks
Standard **antituberculous chemotherapy** plus **prednisolone** (Davidson: 3-month course starting at 60 mg/day, tapered quickly)
Use anticoagulants cautiously; watch for tamponade
Avoid NSAIDs and steroids early (aneurysm, rupture)
High-dose aspirin, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids if severe or prolonged
Antimicrobials + pericardiocentesis, with **surgical drainage** if needed

blocks.title: Admission and activity
items: **Admit high-risk patients:** fever over 38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion, tamponade, or no response to therapy (no NSAID response after about 7 days); leukocytosis is also a warning sign
Uncomplicated cases can be managed as outpatients; most settle in 2–6 weeks
Restrict activity until symptoms and inflammatory markers normalise; competitive athletes avoid exercise for **at least 3 months**
Where the cause is autoimmune (for example SLE), treat the underlying disease with steroids or immunosuppression

blocks.title: Recurrent (relapsing) pericarditis
items: Develops in about **20%** of acute idiopathic cases: **incessant** (recurs within ~6 weeks) or **chronic** (lasting over 3 months)
Treat with **NSAID/aspirin plus colchicine for up to 6 months**
Resistant cases: oral steroids, **IL-1 blockers** (anakinra, rilonacept) or pericardiectomy
Colchicine roughly **halves** refractory or recurrent pericarditis; amiodarone, diltiazem, verapamil and atorvastatin increase its toxicity

blocks.text: **Glucocorticoids increase recurrence.** Reserve them for a known immune cause or for when NSAIDs are contraindicated (Pocket Medicine also lists uraemia and pregnancy). Davidson adds that colchicine and steroids suppress symptoms but **do not speed cure**, whereas Kumar and the quick sources give colchicine routinely.

**Post-MI pericarditis, where the sources disagree:** Davidson advises **opiate analgesia** and avoiding NSAIDs and steroids early (risk of aneurysm and rupture). Pocket Medicine and First Aid prefer **aspirin** over other NSAIDs after MI. Davidson and First Aid both say **steroids should be avoided** in the first days. For the exam, follow Davidson.
**TB prednisolone course:** Davidson gives a **3-month** course (60 mg/day, tapered rapidly) and Kumar gives 60 mg daily for **2–6 weeks**. Quote Davidson.

**Myocarditis** is acute inflammation of the myocardium from an **infectious, toxic or autoimmune** cause. **Viruses are the commonest cause**: about 35 per 1000 Coxsackie infections and 25 per 1000 influenza A/B infections. It may appear **several weeks after** the viral illness. Susceptibility rises with glucocorticoids, immunosuppression, radiation, previous myocardial damage and exercise. Worldwide, **Chagas disease** (Trypanosoma cruzi, South America) is one of the commonest causes.

blocks.title: Causes of myocarditis
rows: Coxsackie, adenovirus, influenza A and B, HIV, parvovirus B19
Young adult after a viral prodrome
SLE, RA, systemic sclerosis, **sarcoidosis**, **giant cell myocarditis**; penicillins, sulphonamides

blocks.title: Presentation
items: Typically a **young adult**: fatigue, palpitations, chest pain, dyspnoea; may mimic **ACS** (chest pain, ECG changes, raised troponin)
Signs: tachycardia, soft heart sounds, **prominent S3**, sometimes a pericardial rub; fever and biventricular failure

Davidson's four patterns: **fulminant** (after a viral prodrome, severe heart failure or cardiogenic shock), **acute** (heart failure that may progress to dilated cardiomyopathy), **chronic active** (rare) and **chronic persistent** (focal infiltrates, chest pain and arrhythmia without ventricular dysfunction)

blocks.title: Investigations
items: Often a **diagnosis of exclusion** after commoner causes of cardiac dysfunction are ruled out; coronary angiography is often done to exclude ischaemia
**Troponin and CK** raised early; ESR and CRP often raised
**ECG** abnormal but non-specific; it may show diffuse concave ST elevation like pericarditis. **AV block** points to Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, giant cell myocarditis or Chagas
**Echo:** LV dysfunction, global or **regional**; LV small in fulminant disease and dilated in chronic disease
**Cardiac MRI** confirms the diagnosis: T2 oedema and **patchy mid-wall/epicardial gadolinium enhancement**

**Endomyocardial biopsy** is the gold standard but is reserved for fulminant or deteriorating cases, high-grade AV block, sustained VT, or suspected giant cell/eosinophilic disease. Lymphocytes suggest a viral cause, neutrophils bacterial, eosinophils hypersensitivity

blocks.title: Impaired cardiac function and outcome
items: Usually **self-limiting** within weeks, with a good immediate prognosis
Death can come from **ventricular arrhythmia** or rapidly progressive heart failure; it is a cause of **sudden death in young athletes**

Can progress to **dilated cardiomyopathy**; a late autoimmune reaction to viral myocarditis probably explains a large share of DCM. In Chagas, DCM with heart block and ventricular arrhythmias appears 10–20 years after the acute infection
**Giant cell myocarditis** (linked to sarcoidosis, thymoma, autoimmunity) runs a rapid course with a poor prognosis

blocks.title: Management
items: **Supportive:** treat heart failure and arrhythmias in the usual way (do not start HF drugs during shock)
**Avoid intense exertion**: it may trigger fatal ventricular arrhythmias. Kumar advises bed rest in the acute phase and **no athletic activity for 6 months**
**No proven benefit from steroids or immunosuppression** in viral myocarditis; immunosuppression **is** used for giant cell, eosinophilic and collagen-vascular myocarditis
Refractory cases: mechanical support (ventricular assist device, ECMO) or, rarely, **transplantation**
Chagas heart disease: **amiodarone** for ventricular arrhythmias

blocks.text: **Viral serology:** Essentials of K&C says rising viral titres support the diagnosis, but Kumar says serology is rarely helpful. Davidson relies on troponin, echo, cardiac MRI and occasionally biopsy, so do not offer serology as the confirmatory test.

blocks.note: Look at: patchy mid-wall and epicardial late gadolinium enhancement in acute myocarditis.
Look at: normal myocardium compared with myocarditis, where interstitial inflammatory cells are increased.

cards.front: Share of pericarditis that is tuberculous in developing countries and in HIV-positive patients?
cards.back: Over **50%** in developing countries and over **90%** in HIV-positive patients (under 5% in developed countries).

cards.front: In what settings does uraemic pericarditis occur, and what features accompany it?
cards.back: Severe pre-terminal uraemia or **under-dialysis**. It is often accompanied by a **haemorrhagic effusion** and **atrial arrhythmias**, and there is a risk of tamponade.
Weeks to months after MI: **fever, pericarditis and pleurisy**, probably autoimmune.

cards.front: How many of the four features are needed to diagnose acute pericarditis clinically?
cards.back: **Two of four:** typical pleuritic, positional pain; friction rub; typical ECG changes; pericardial effusion.

cards.front: Which ECG sign is a very specific indicator of acute pericarditis?
cards.back: **PR-segment depression** (with PR elevation in aVR), alongside widespread concave ST elevation.
An exaggerated inspiratory **fall in systolic BP of ≥10 mmHg**; in severe tamponade the pulse may disappear in inspiration.
**Hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised JVP**, but it is often incomplete.
**Late diastolic RA collapse, early diastolic RV collapse**, inspiratory septal shift into the LV, plethoric IVC (<50% inspiratory collapse), expiratory hepatic-vein flow reversal.

cards.front: Tamponade from aortic dissection or free-wall rupture: what is the treatment?
cards.back: **Emergency surgery**, because needle aspiration can provoke fatal further bleeding.

cards.front: When should you suspect constrictive pericarditis?
cards.back: **Unexplained right heart failure with a small heart**, or ascites and hepatomegaly with distended neck veins.

cards.front: Constriction: CT/CMR pericardial thickness and catheter finding?
cards.back: Pericardium **≥4 mm**; catheterisation shows **equal LV and RV end-diastolic pressures** with a dip-and-plateau trace.
Standard **antituberculous chemotherapy** plus a **3-month prednisolone course** (60 mg/day, tapered rapidly).

cards.front: Why avoid glucocorticoids in idiopathic pericarditis?
cards.back: They **increase recurrence**. Reserve them for immune causes or when NSAIDs are contraindicated.

cards.front: Analgesia for pericarditis on day 2–3 after MI (Davidson)?
cards.back: **Opiate-based analgesia**. Avoid NSAIDs and steroids early because they may promote aneurysm and myocardial rupture.

cards.front: Cardiac MRI findings in acute myocarditis?
cards.back: Myocardial **oedema on T2** images and **patchy mid-wall/epicardial gadolinium enhancement**.

cards.front: Myocarditis with AV block: which causes?
cards.back: **Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, giant cell myocarditis, Chagas disease** (also diphtheria).

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man living in sub-Saharan Africa has advanced HIV infection. Over 6 weeks he has developed evening fevers, drenching sweats, 7 kg weight loss and increasing breathlessness. Echo shows a large pericardial effusion, and a left pleural effusion is also present.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of the pericardial effusion?
questions.explanation: A subacute illness with **evening fever, night sweats, weight loss** and a pericardial plus pleural effusion in **HIV** is classic tuberculous pericarditis. TB causes over 90% of pericarditis in HIV-positive patients and is the commonest cause of pericardial disease in HIV worldwide.
whyNot: Viral pericarditis is acute and short-lived, without weeks of constitutional symptoms.
Kaposi sarcoma can cause effusions in HIV, but TB is far commoner and fits the systemic picture.
Septic pneumococcal pericarditis is uncommon and presents acutely with toxicity, not over 6 weeks.
Nothing suggests renal failure.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with end-stage kidney disease has missed several haemodialysis sessions. She has dull chest discomfort, a scratchy sound at the left sternal edge and new atrial fibrillation. Echo shows a moderate effusion, and a diagnostic tap returns bloodstained fluid. She has no history of cancer or recent MI.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Under-dialysis** is the key clue. Uraemic pericarditis typically comes with a **haemorrhagic effusion** and **atrial arrhythmias**, and there is a risk of tamponade. It is treated by intensifying dialysis.
whyNot: Malignancy also gives haemorrhagic effusions, but there is no cancer history and the missed dialysis explains the picture.
Dressler syndrome requires a preceding MI.
Hypothyroid effusions are transudates without a rub or haemorrhage.
Viral pericarditis would not explain the link with missed dialysis or a bloody effusion.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has had sharp central chest pain for 2 days, starting after a cold. It is worse lying flat and better leaning forward. The ECG shows ST elevation in leads I, II, aVL and V2–V6.
questions.leadIn: Which additional ECG finding most strongly favours acute pericarditis over STEMI?
options: Pathological Q waves in II, III and aVF
Reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF
questions.explanation: **PR depression** is a very specific sign of acute pericarditis. The other pericarditic features are **concave** ST elevation spread across anterior **and** inferior leads, with reciprocal depression only in aVR/V1.
whyNot: Q waves indicate infarction, not pericardial inflammation.
Reciprocal ST depression in opposite leads suggests a territorial infarct.
Convex (dome-shaped) ST elevation is the infarct pattern.
Hyperacute T waves are an early sign of infarction.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student has pleuritic central chest pain eased by sitting forward. A three-component scratchy sound is heard at the lower left sternal border. The ECG is normal, echo shows no effusion and the troponin is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: Acute pericarditis can be diagnosed clinically
Pericarditis is excluded because the ECG is normal
Pericarditis is excluded because there is no effusion
Pericarditis cannot be diagnosed without a raised troponin
Pericarditis can only be confirmed by cardiac MRI
questions.explanation: A clinical diagnosis needs **two of four** features: typical pain, friction rub, ECG changes and effusion. Typical pain plus a **rub** is enough, and a rub is diagnostic on its own.
whyNot: ECG changes are only one of the four criteria.
An effusion is not required.
Troponin rises only when there is myocardial involvement (myopericarditis).
Imaging is not needed when two clinical criteria are met.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with lung cancer is breathless. BP is 86/60 mmHg, pulse 120/min, JVP 12 cm and heart sounds are soft. Her radial pulse almost disappears with each inspiration, and systolic pressure falls by 20 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: What best explains the inspiratory change in her pulse?
options: Inspiratory RV filling within a fixed pericardial space pushes the septum left and reduces LV filling
Inspiration reduces venous return to the right heart
Severe aortic stenosis limits stroke volume
Vagal slowing of the heart during inspiration
A calcified pericardium halts filling in early diastole
questions.explanation: This is **pulsus paradoxus** (inspiratory systolic fall ≥10 mmHg) from tamponade. The fluid confines both ventricles, so extra inspiratory RV filling happens **at the LV's expense**, and LV stroke volume falls.
whyNot: Inspiration increases, not decreases, right-heart venous return.
Aortic stenosis does not produce respiratory variation in pulse volume.
Sinus arrhythmia changes rate, not pulse volume, and is not paradoxical.
That describes constriction physiology; this patient has an acute malignant effusion picture.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old hypertensive man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back and then collapses. BP 78/50 mmHg, JVP grossly raised, heart sounds muffled. Bedside echo shows a pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse and a dilated aortic root containing an intimal flap.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate definitive management?
options: Echo-guided needle pericardiocentesis as definitive treatment
Observation with repeat echo in 24 hours
questions.explanation: This is tamponade from **aortic dissection**. Needle aspiration can provoke **fatal further bleeding**, so **emergency surgery** is the treatment of choice. Any drainage only buys time.
whyNot: Aspiration in dissection or rupture risks fatal bleeding and is not definitive.
Beta-blockers are avoided in tamponade because they remove the compensatory tachycardia.
Thrombolysis would be catastrophic in dissection and haemopericardium.
Tamponade is an emergency; delay is fatal.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man was treated for tuberculous pericarditis 2 years ago. He now has 6 months of abdominal swelling, leg oedema and fatigue, but little breathlessness. The JVP is raised with a rapid y descent and rises on inspiration, an early diastolic sound is heard, and the CXR shows a small heart.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation finding would most support the likely diagnosis?
options: Pericardial thickness of 6 mm on CT
Dilated LV with ejection fraction of 20%
Large effusion with late diastolic right atrial collapse
questions.explanation: Right heart failure with a **small heart**, rapid y descent, Kussmaul sign and a **knock** after TB pericarditis means **constriction**. A pericardial thickness of **≥4 mm** on CT/CMR supports it.
whyNot: A dilated, poorly contracting LV indicates dilated cardiomyopathy, not constriction.
Diastolic chamber collapse with a large effusion indicates tamponade.
Constriction gives a **high** SAAG (post-hepatic portal hypertension).
Coronary disease does not explain a small heart with isolated right-sided congestion.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man who had cardiac surgery 3 years ago has ascites, oedema and a raised JVP. Echo shows septal bounce, about 30% respiratory variation in mitral inflow and a tissue-Doppler e′ of 14 cm/s. NT-proBNP is only mildly raised and CT shows a thick pericardium.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Normal/high e′, marked respiratory variation, septal bounce and a thick pericardium** favour constriction (after cardiac surgery). Restrictive cardiomyopathy gives a low e′ (<8 cm/s), little respiratory variation, high NT-proBNP and a normal pericardium.
whyNot: Restriction has low e′, <10% respiratory variation, high NT-proBNP and a normal pericardium.
There is no effusion described.
Dilated cardiomyopathy has a dilated, poorly contracting LV.
Cirrhosis does not raise the JVP or thicken the pericardium.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has typical acute pericarditis after a viral illness. She is afebrile, echo shows no effusion and she is otherwise well.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Davidson recommends **aspirin 600 mg 6 times daily** (indometacin if a stronger drug is needed). Kumar uses aspirin or ibuprofen plus colchicine for 3 months. Uncomplicated cases are treated as outpatients.
whyNot: Steroids increase recurrence and are reserved for immune causes.
There is no effusion to drain.
This is not purulent pericarditis.
Anticoagulation has no role and risks haemopericardium.

questions.stem: On day 3 after an anterior STEMI, a 59-year-old man develops a new sharp chest pain, worse on inspiration and when lying back, at the same site as his infarct pain. A pericardial rub is heard.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is the most appropriate analgesia?
questions.explanation: Early post-infarct pericarditis peaks on days 2–3. Davidson advises **opiate analgesia**, because NSAIDs and steroids early after MI may increase aneurysm formation and **myocardial rupture**. Some quick sources prefer aspirin, but follow Davidson.
whyNot: NSAIDs early after MI may promote aneurysm and rupture.
Indometacin is an NSAID with the same early post-MI risk.
Steroids early after MI predispose to ventricular wall rupture.
Steroids early after MI predispose to ventricular wall rupture.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has chest pain and breathlessness 2 weeks after a flu-like illness. Troponin is raised, the ECG shows diffuse ST elevation, coronary angiography is normal and echo shows mild regional LV hypokinesia.
questions.leadIn: Which test is recommended to confirm the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is myocarditis. **Cardiac MRI** confirms it by showing myocardial oedema and **patchy mid-wall/epicardial gadolinium enhancement**. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard but is reserved for fulminant or deteriorating cases.
whyNot: Viral serology is rarely helpful in diagnosis.
Exercise testing is inappropriate in acute myocarditis and does not diagnose it.
CXR may show cardiomegaly but cannot confirm myocardial inflammation.
The coronaries are already normal.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old semi-professional footballer is recovering from viral myocarditis. He has mild LV impairment and no arrhythmia, and asks when he can train again.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Standard heart-failure therapy and no competitive sport for about 6 months
Return to training once troponin is normal
questions.explanation: Treatment is **supportive**. Intense exertion may trigger fatal ventricular arrhythmias (myocarditis causes sudden death in young athletes), so Kumar advises **avoiding athletics for 6 months**. Steroids and immunosuppressants have no proven benefit in viral myocarditis.
whyNot: Steroids have no proven benefit in viral myocarditis.
Immunosuppression is for giant cell, eosinophilic or collagen-vascular myocarditis, not viral.
An early return to exertion risks arrhythmic death.
Specific antimicrobial therapy is rarely possible and is not standard.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the likeliest cause. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man had an anterior MI 5 weeks ago. He now has fever, pleuritic pain on both sides of the chest and a pericardial rub. ESR is raised.
items.explanation: Step 1: pericarditis **weeks** after MI, not days, rules out early post-infarct pericarditis (days 2–3). Step 2: fever plus **pleurisy** plus pericarditis is **Dressler syndrome**, an autoimmune reaction.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with heart failure has taken hydralazine for 18 months. She develops arthralgia, a pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial rub. ANA is positive.
items.explanation: Step 1: arthralgia, serositis and a positive ANA suggest a lupus picture. Step 2: **hydralazine** (like procainamide and isoniazid) causes **drug-induced** autoimmune pericarditis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old previously well man had a coryzal illness a week ago. He now has sharp chest pain relieved by leaning forward, a rub, and widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation.
items.explanation: A young adult with a preceding viral illness and no other cause fits **idiopathic (presumed viral)** pericarditis, which accounts for most cases.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old HIV-negative man from a TB-endemic region has 2 months of fever, weight loss and breathlessness. Echo shows a large effusion. Pericardial fluid grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis. There is no pericardial calcification.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Antituberculous chemotherapy plus a tapering course of prednisolone
questions.explanation: Step 1: the cause is confirmed as **tuberculous pericarditis** (culture-positive fluid). Step 2: it needs standard **antituberculous chemotherapy**. Step 3: Davidson adds a **3-month prednisolone course** (60 mg/day, tapered rapidly), which improves outcome. Step 4: without calcification, surgery is not first-line; pericardiectomy is reserved for constriction that fails to improve on treatment.
whyNot: Davidson states that adding prednisolone improves outcome.
This treats idiopathic pericarditis and leaves the infection untreated.
Early pericardiectomy is for calcified tuberculous constriction, not an uncomplicated effusion.
Steroids without anti-TB drugs would let the infection progress.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the likeliest diagnosis. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has been stabbed just to the left of the sternum. BP 78/50 mmHg, pulse 130/min, neck veins distended and heart sounds quiet. The trachea is central, breath sounds are equal and the lungs are clear.
items.explanation: Step 1: shock with a **raised JVP** and quiet heart sounds (Beck triad). Step 2: a central trachea and equal breath sounds argue against tension pneumothorax. Penetrating trauma causing rapid haemopericardium gives **tamponade**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman had mediastinal radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 15 years ago. For a year her abdomen and legs have been swelling, with little breathlessness. The JVP is raised with a brisk y descent and rises on inspiration, there is an early diastolic knock, and the heart is small on CXR.
items.explanation: Radiation is a high-risk cause of **constriction**. Right-sided congestion with a small heart, rapid y descent, Kussmaul sign and knock is the classic picture. The raised JVP rules out cirrhosis as the cause of the ascites.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had palpitations and breathlessness since a diarrhoeal illness 2 weeks ago. She has a third heart sound. Troponin is raised, echo shows reduced global LV function with a normal pericardium, and the coronary arteries are normal.
items.explanation: A young adult with a **viral prodrome**, raised troponin, S3 and new LV dysfunction with normal coronaries has **acute myocarditis**.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man with lung cancer is mildly breathless. BP is 132/80 mmHg with no inspiratory fall. Heart sounds are soft, the apex is impalpable and there is dullness beneath the left scapula. Echo shows a 1.5 cm circumferential effusion with no chamber collapse.
items.explanation: Soft sounds, impalpable apex and **Ewart sign** indicate an effusion, but normal BP, no pulsus paradoxus and **no chamber collapse** mean there is no tamponade.

questions.theme: Investigations in pericardial and myocardial disease
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the single most useful next investigation. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Diagnostic pericardiocentesis with AFB culture, ADA and TB PCR
Simultaneous right and left heart catheterisation

items.stem: A 26-year-old man has typical pericarditic chest pain, a friction rub and saddle-shaped ST elevation. Before deciding on outpatient care, the team wants to know whether there is fluid around the heart.
items.explanation: **Echocardiography** is the test of choice for effusion and should be done in every patient with acute pericarditis.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman who recently arrived from a TB-endemic country has weight loss, night sweats and a moderate pericardial effusion without tamponade. The cause is unknown.
items.explanation: Suspected **tuberculous** effusion is an indication for a **diagnostic tap**: smear and culture for tubercle bacilli, plus ADA and TB PCR.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man is still strongly suspected of having tuberculous pericarditis, although smear, culture and PCR on two pericardial aspirates were all negative.
items.explanation: When TB is suspected but the aspirate is **non-diagnostic**, the next step is **pericardial biopsy**.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man with fulminant myocarditis is deteriorating despite inotropes. He develops complete heart block and sustained VT, and giant cell myocarditis is suspected.
items.explanation: Step 1: a fulminant, deteriorating course with high-grade AV block and VT. Step 2: suspected **giant cell** myocarditis needs tissue diagnosis because it is treated with immunosuppression, so **endomyocardial biopsy** is indicated.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most appropriate management. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: NSAID plus colchicine for up to 6 months
Treatment of underlying SLE with steroids or immunosuppression

items.stem: A 47-year-old man is recovering from a severe pneumonia when he develops rigors, pericardial pain and an effusion. The aspirate is turbid and Gram-positive cocci are seen. He is haemodynamically stable.
items.explanation: **Purulent** pericarditis needs **drainage**, preferably surgical, plus systemic antibiotics.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with lymphoma is acutely breathless. BP 80/50 mmHg, inspiratory systolic fall 18 mmHg. Echo shows a large effusion with early diastolic RV collapse. There is no aortic dissection or trauma.
items.explanation: This is **tamponade** from a malignant effusion with no rupture or dissection. **Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis** is the emergency treatment.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has idiopathic constrictive pericarditis confirmed by CT and catheterisation. He keeps worsening despite maximal loop diuretic and spironolactone.
items.explanation: Medical therapy only controls congestion. **Pericardiectomy** is the definitive treatment, and Kumar advises doing it early in non-TB cases, before myocardial atrophy sets in.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has her third episode of idiopathic pericarditis in 6 months, each recurring within weeks of stopping ibuprofen. There is no effusion and no autoimmune disease.
items.explanation: Step 1: repeated relapses mean **recurrent (incessant) pericarditis**. Step 2: treat with an **NSAID plus colchicine for up to 6 months**. Steroids increase recurrence and are kept for resistant cases.

questions.theme: ECG findings in pericardial and myocardial disease
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the ECG finding you would most expect. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Regional convex ST elevation with reciprocal ST depression
Diffuse T-wave inversion with isoelectric ST segments
Low-voltage QRS complexes with electrical alternans
Low-voltage QRS with generalised T flattening
No classic pericarditic ST or PR changes
Deep Q waves in II, III and aVF

items.stem: A 27-year-old man presents on the first day of sharp, positional chest pain that began after a flu-like illness. A rub is audible.
items.explanation: Stage I of acute pericarditis: **widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression**.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man had viral pericarditis 3 weeks ago. His ST segments returned to baseline last week, but today's follow-up ECG shows a new change spread across most leads, with the ST segments still isoelectric.
items.explanation: After ST segments return to baseline (stage II), **diffuse T-wave inversion** follows (stage III). In pericarditis, unlike STEMI, T waves invert only after the ST segments have normalised.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease who has missed dialysis has a pericardial rub and a moderate effusion.
items.explanation: Step 1: the setting is **uraemic pericarditis**. Step 2: it is mostly fibrin deposition without epicardial inflammation, so the classic diffuse ST elevation and PR depression are usually **absent**.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman who hikes in wooded areas had an expanding red rash 2 months ago. She now has dizzy spells, a slow pulse and features of myopericarditis.
items.explanation: **Lyme disease** causes myopericarditis in about 5% of cases, often with **AV block**, which can be complete.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has BP 85/50 mmHg, a raised JVP and a 20 mmHg inspiratory fall in systolic pressure.
items.explanation: Tamponade from a large malignant effusion: **low-voltage complexes and electrical alternans** as the heart swings in the fluid (plus sinus tachycardia).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man on haemodialysis has been missing sessions. He has a pericardial rub and a moderate non-haemorrhagic effusion on echo. BP is 128/76 mmHg, with no pulsus paradoxus or chamber collapse.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Uraemic pericarditis often settles with **intensive dialysis**. In stable, non-haemorrhagic tamponade in renal failure, dialysis is preferred to aspiration. Anticoagulants must be used cautiously because these effusions can be haemorrhagic.
whyNot: He is stable without tamponade; aspiration is not needed.
Steroids are not the primary treatment; correcting uraemia is.
Anticoagulation risks haemorrhagic effusion and tamponade.
Pericardiectomy is for constriction.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman had idiopathic pericarditis 3 months ago, treated with ibuprofen alone. After 6 symptom-free weeks the typical pain and rub return. There is no effusion and no fever.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: NSAID plus colchicine for up to 6 months
questions.explanation: This is **recurrent pericarditis** (about 20% of cases). First-line treatment is an **NSAID/aspirin plus colchicine for up to 6 months**. Colchicine roughly halves further recurrences.
whyNot: Steroids increase recurrence and are kept for resistant cases.
Surgery is a last resort for resistant relapses.
There is no evidence of bacterial infection.
Anticoagulation has no role.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the complication that best explains the picture. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man grew up in rural Bolivia and had a febrile illness with heart failure as a child. He is now breathless; echo shows a large, poorly contracting left ventricle, and his ECG shows RBBB.
items.explanation: Step 1: childhood exposure in South America suggests acute **Chagas** myocarditis. Step 2: patients often recover and then develop **dilated cardiomyopathy 10–20 years later**, with conduction disease and arrhythmias.

items.stem: A 19-year-old rugby player is recovering from myocarditis after a viral illness and ignores advice to rest. He collapses during a match and cannot be resuscitated.
items.explanation: Myocarditis is a recognised cause of **sudden death in young athletes** from ventricular arrhythmia, which is why intense exertion is avoided.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman was treated for a tuberculous pericardial effusion 18 months ago; echo at the time showed fibrous strands in the fluid. She now has ascites, a raised JVP that rises on inspiration and a small heart on CXR.
items.explanation: An organising (stranded) tuberculous effusion commonly progresses to **constriction**: right heart failure with a small heart and Kussmaul sign.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with breast cancer is increasingly breathless, with a raised JVP and soft heart sounds. Echo shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion.
questions.leadIn: Which additional echo finding most strongly indicates tamponade physiology?
options: Early diastolic collapse of the right ventricle
IVC collapsing by more than 50% on inspiration
Septal bounce with a thickened pericardium
Global LV hypokinesia with ejection fraction of 25%
Biatrial enlargement with thickened LV walls
questions.explanation: Signs of tamponade on echo: **early diastolic RV collapse**, late diastolic RA collapse, inspiratory septal shift into the LV, a dilated IVC collapsing <50%, and expiratory hepatic-vein flow reversal.
whyNot: A normally collapsing IVC implies low right-sided pressure, arguing against tamponade.
Septal bounce with a thick pericardium points to constriction.
This describes systolic dysfunction, not compression.
This pattern suggests restrictive cardiomyopathy.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the likeliest cause of myocarditis. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia started a new antipsychotic 3 weeks ago. He now has fever, tachycardia, chest pain and a raised troponin.
items.explanation: **Clozapine** is a recognised drug cause of myocarditis, typically within weeks of starting it.

items.stem: A 41-year-old forestry worker had an expanding target-like rash after a tick bite 6 weeks ago. He now has chest pain, a raised troponin and second-degree AV block.
items.explanation: Tick bite plus erythema migrans means **Lyme disease** (Borrelia burgdorferi); about 5% develop myopericarditis, often with **AV block**.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman who grew up in rural Brazil has dysphagia from a dilated oesophagus, RBBB on ECG and an LV apical aneurysm on echo.
items.explanation: Step 1: megaoesophagus plus RBBB and an **apical aneurysm**. Step 2: this combination in someone from South America indicates chronic **Chagas** heart disease (T. cruzi).

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with a thymoma has rapidly progressive heart failure and recurrent VT. Endomyocardial biopsy shows multinucleated giant cells.
items.explanation: **Giant cell myocarditis** is associated with thymoma, sarcoidosis and autoimmunity; it runs a fulminant course and is treated with immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has had two pericardiocenteses for tamponade in the past month; each time the fluid has re-accumulated.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate procedure to prevent further tamponade?
questions.explanation: Recurrent effusions, most often malignant in the UK, are managed with **pericardial fenestration**: a window that lets fluid drain slowly into the surrounding tissues. It can be done percutaneously or surgically.
whyNot: Repeated taps carry cumulative risks and do not stop re-accumulation.
Colchicine treats inflammatory pericarditis, not malignant effusions.
Diuretics reduce preload and can worsen tamponade.
Coronary surgery has no relevance to a malignant effusion.

ospe.identify: Widespread **concave ST elevation** in anterior and inferior leads, matching no single coronary territory: **acute (viral) pericarditis**, not STEMI.
A large **circumferential echo-free space** around the LV: **pericardial effusion**. Next, look for diastolic RA/RV collapse to judge tamponade.
Enlarged **globular cardiac silhouette** on CXR, with CT showing circumferential fluid and no calcification: **pericardial effusion**.
QRS amplitude alternating beat to beat: **electrical alternans** from a heart swinging in a **large effusion / tamponade**.
A dense rim of **pericardial calcification** on a lateral CXR: **chronic constrictive pericarditis** (classically after TB).
A large **tuberculous effusion with fibrous strands** on echo, meaning the exudate is organising and is likely to progress to **constriction**.
**Patchy mid-wall and epicardial late gadolinium enhancement** on cardiac MRI: **acute myocarditis**.
